idiom_name: block-taking method with ensure (File.open's block form; def with_resource; ... yield ... ensure ... end)
implementation_notes: Ruby has no destructor - ObjectSpace.define_finalizer runs at GC time and cannot be the release point - so the classic owner object is replaced by an idiom: a method acquires the resource, yields it to a block and releases it in an ensure clause, which runs on normal return, break, next, return and exception alike. The standard library's own resources are written that way: File.open/IO.open with a block closes the file when the block terminates, and the documented source shows the yield wrapped in rb_ensure(rb_yield, io, io_close, io), so the block form is the deterministic one and a bare File.open with a later explicit close is the leak-prone one. For anything outside the stdlib, write the shape once as a method (def with_conn(pool) ... yield conn ... ensure pool.checkin(conn) if conn ... end) and keep the release idempotent.
code_sketch:
def with_connection(pool)
  conn = pool.checkout
  yield conn
ensure
  pool.checkin(conn) if conn      # return, break, raise: always
end

# stdlib equivalent: File.open(path) { |f| f.read }
pitfalls: ensure does not run when the process ends abruptly (exit!, System.kill, kill -9): handles that must survive a shutdown still need an explicit release on that path.

A block that rescues and retries, or a method re-entered from inside its own block, can reach the release twice; keep the release idempotent or guard it, because ensure only guarantees running, not running once.

ObjectSpace.define_finalizer is not RAII: the finalizer runs at GC time (possibly never before exit) and a finalizer that closes over the object keeps it alive, so finalizers belong in libraries as leak warnings, never as the release mechanism.
